An operating system (OS) is system software that manages computer hardware, software resources, and provides common services for computer programs.
Time-sharing operating systems schedule tasks for efficient use of the system and may also include accounting software for cost allocation of processor time, mass storage, printing, and other resources.
For hardware functions such as input and output and memory allocation, the operating system acts as an intermediary between programs and the computer hardware.

In mathematics and computer science, an algorithm is a finite sequence of rigorous instructions, typically used to solve a class of specific problems or to perform a computation.
Algorithms are used as specifications for performing calculations and data processing.
More advanced algorithms can perform automated deductions (referred to as automated reasoning) and use mathematical and logical tests to direct the code execution through various routes.

 Abstract 
 
The Event and Room Occupancy Management System is a web-based application designed to help 
students  and  college  administrators  efficiently manage  room  availability,  event  scheduling,  and 
participant registrations within a college campus. Students often face difficulty finding available 
rooms  during  college  hours,  while  events  such  as  hackathons,  workshops,  seminars,  and 
competitions may experience unexpected increases in participants due to spot registrations. These 
situations  can  lead  to  room  allocation  conflicts,  overcrowding,  and  inefficient  utilization  of 
available spaces. 
The  proposed  system  provides  a  user-friendly  web  interface  through which  users  can  view 
available rooms, check room capacity and schedules, register for events, and access relevant event 
information.  Administrators  are  able  to  create  and  manage  events,  allocate  rooms,  monitor 
registrations, and track expected and actual occupancy. The system also helps identify scheduling 
conflicts  and  capacity  issues,  allowing  administrators  to  make  better  decisions  regarding  room 
allocation. 
The  application  uses  a  React-based  frontend,  a  Node.js  and  Express.js  backend,  and  a  MySQL 
relational  database  for  storing  and  managing  system  information.  The  database  maintains 
relationships between users, rooms, events, registrations, bookings, and schedules while ensuring 
data consistency and integrity through primary keys, foreign keys, and validation constraints. The 
system was built and tested in incremental phases — from schema design through authentication, 
room and event management, booking logic, occupancy tracking, and finally a full React frontend 
for  both  students  and  administrators — with  each  phase  verified  against  a  running  MySQL 
database  before  the  next  was  built.  The  system  achieves  its  aim  of  improving  campus  resource 
utilization,  reducing  scheduling  conflicts,  providing  better  visibility  of  room  availability,  and 
offering a centralized platform for efficient event and room management.

CHAPTER -1 INTRODUCTION 
1.1 Background of the Project 
Colleges  routinely  run  a  large  number  of  events — workshops,  seminars,  hackathons,  club 
meetings,  and  competitions — that  all  compete  for  the  same  limited  pool  of  rooms.  In  most 
departments,  room  booking  is  still  coordinated  informally:  through  phone  calls,  WhatsApp 
messages, a shared spreadsheet, or a notice pinned outside the administration office. This works 
reasonably  well  when  activity  is  low,  but  breaks  down  quickly  during  periods  of  high  demand, 
such as a hackathon that unexpectedly attracts far more participants than a room can seat, or two 
departments independently booking the same seminar hall for overlapping time slots. 
The  Event  and  Room  Occupancy  Management  System  was  built  to  replace  this  informal 
coordination with a single, database-backed source of truth. Every room, every event, and every 
registration  is  stored  in  one  relational  database,  and  the  system  itself — not  a  human  cross-
checking  a  spreadsheet — is  responsible  for  detecting  when  a room  is  already  booked,  when  a 
room is too small for an event, or when a student tries to register twice for the same event. 
1.2 Problem Statement 
Given  a  college  campus  with  a  fixed  number  of  rooms  of  varying  capacity  and  type,  and  a 
continuous stream of events being scheduled by different organizers, the system must answer three 
questions  reliably  and  in  real  time:  which  rooms  are  free  for  a  given  date  and  time,  whether  a 
specific  room  can  be  safely  assigned  to  a  specific  event,  and  whether  a  specific  student  can  be 
allowed  to  register  for  a  specific  event.  Answering  these  questions  manually  does  not  scale,  is 
error-prone, and gives students no visibility into room availability until they physically check. 
1.3 Scope of the Project 
The system covers the full lifecycle of a campus event from the room's perspective: adding and 
maintaining a directory of rooms (with capacity, type, equipment, and status); creating and editing 
events; assigning a room to an event only after checking its status, capacity, and existing schedule; 
students registering for events subject to duplicate and capacity checks; an audit trail of booking 
actions; and a simple occupancy-tracking mechanism for recording actual attendance after an event 
takes  place.  Payment  processing,  multi-campus  support,  and  a  native  mobile  application  were 
treated as out of scope for this submission. 
1.4 Objectives 
• Provide real-time room availability for any requested date and time window. 
• Prevent a room from ever being double-booked, using a single, consistently-applied overlap rule. 
• Enforce registration rules: no duplicate registrations, and  no registrations  beyond a room's  capacity 
once one is assigned. 
• Give  administrators  a  single  dashboard  to  manage  rooms,  events,  bookings,  registrations,  and 
occupancy. 
• Automatically calculate an occupancy percentage and status (Normal / High / Near Capacity / Over 
Capacity) for completed events. 

Page 6 
 
• Secure  the  system  with  role-based  access,  so  student  accounts  can  never  reach  admin-only 
functionality. 
 
1.5 Importance of the Application 
By  centralizing  room  and  event  data,  the  system  removes  the  guesswork  from  room  allocation. 
Administrators  gain  a  live  view  of  which  rooms  are  occupied  at  any  given  moment  and  which 
upcoming events have a capacity mismatch, letting them intervene before an event happens rather 
than discovering a problem on the day. Students  gain the ability to check  room availability  and 
register for events themselves, without needing to contact an administrator directly. 
1.6 Target Users / Audience 
The  system  serves  two  roles.  Students  use  it  to  browse  and  search  events,  view  event  details, 
register for events, track their own registrations, and check room availability. Administrators use 
it  to  manage  the  room  inventory,  create  and  edit  events,  assign  rooms  to  events,  monitor  all 
bookings and registrations across the campus, and track occupancy after events conclude. 

Page 7 
 
CHAPTER 2: SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS 
2.1 Hardware Requirements 
The  application  has  modest  hardware  requirements,  since  both  the  Node.js  backend  and  the 
MySQL  database  are  lightweight  relative  to  the  small  dataset  a  single  campus  generates.  A 
development or demonstration machine with a dual-core processor, 4 GB of RAM, and roughly 
500 MB of free disk space (for Node modules, MySQL data files, and project source) is sufficient 
to run the entire stack — frontend, backend, and database — on one computer. 
2.2 Software Requirements 
• Node.js 18 or later, with npm 
• MySQL 8.0 or later 
• A modern web browser (Chrome, Edge, or Firefox) 
• Git, for version control 
• MySQL Workbench and Visual Studio Code, for development (optional but recommended) 
2.3 Development Tools and Frameworks 
React.js (bootstrapped with Vite) was used for the frontend; Node.js with the Express.js framework 
for the backend REST API; MySQL as the relational database, accessed through the mysql2 driver; 
Postman for API testing and documentation; and Git with GitHub for source control. VS Code was 
the  primary  development  environment,  and  MySQL  Workbench  was  used  for  inspecting  and 
verifying the database schema and data directly. 
 

Page 8 
 
CHAPTER 3: TECHNOLOGY STACK 
3.1 Frontend 
The frontend is a single-page application built with React.js and bundled using Vite. React Router 
handles client-side navigation between the public (login/register), student, and admin areas, and 
Axios is used as the single HTTP client for every API call, wrapped in one central service module 
per  backend  resource  (rooms,  events,  registrations,  bookings,  occupancy).  Styling  is  plain  CSS 
with a small set of reusable design tokens (colors, spacing, card/table/badge styles) rather than a 
heavyweight UI framework, keeping the codebase easy to read and modify. 
3.2 Backend 
The backend is a REST API built with Node.js and Express.js, organized into routes, controllers, 
and models — routes declare the URL and required role, controllers hold the request/response and 
validation  logic,  and  models  hold  the raw  SQL.  This  separation  keeps  each  file  focused  on  one 
responsibility and makes the codebase straightforward to navigate and explain. 
3.3 Database 
MySQL 8 stores all persistent data across seven related tables (users, rooms, events, registrations, 
room_schedules, bookings, and occupancy_records). Referential integrity is enforced with foreign 
keys, uniqueness with UNIQUE constraints (e.g. one email per user, one registration per student 
per event), and data validity with CHECK constraints (e.g. no negative capacity, start time before 
end time). 
3.4 Version Control 
Git was used throughout development for version control, with the project structured as a single 
repository containing both the client and server codebases, hosted on GitHub. 
3.5 Authentication and Security Libraries 
Passwords are hashed with bcrypt (10 salt rounds) before being stored — plain-text passwords are 
never written to the database. Login sessions are stateless JSON Web Tokens (JWT), signed with 
a server-side secret and carrying only a user's ID, role, and name. Express middleware verifies this 
token on every protected route and enforces role-based access, ensuring student accounts cannot 
reach admin-only endpoints even if a request is crafted by hand. 

Page 9 
 
 
CHAPTER 4: SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE 
4.1 High-Level Architecture Diagram 
The  system  follows  a  standard  three-tier  architecture,  cleanly  separating  the  user  interface,  the 
business logic, and the persisted data. Figure 4.1 shows the three layers and how a request flows 
between them. 
 
4.2 Description of Each Layer 
The  Presentation  Layer  is  the  React  single-page  application.  It  never  talks  to  MySQL  directly; 
every piece of data it shows comes from calling the REST API over HTTP. During development, 
Vite's built-in proxy forwards any request the frontend makes to “/api/...” straight through to the 
Express server, so the browser never needs to know the backend's actual port or address. 
The Application Layer is the Express.js REST API. Incoming requests pass through authentication 
middleware (which verifies the JWT and attaches the requesting user's identity and role), then into 
a controller that validates the request and applies business rules — for example, checking a room's 
status,  capacity,  and  existing  schedule  before  allowing  it  to be  assigned  to  an  event — before 
finally reading or writing data through a model. 
The  Data  Layer  is  the  MySQL  database,  accessed  through  a  connection  pool  (via  the  mysql2 
driver) rather than a single long-lived connection, so multiple requests can be served concurrently 
without waiting on each other unnecessarily. 
4.3 Deployment Architecture 
For development and demonstration purposes, all three layers run as separate local processes on a 
single machine: the Express server listens on port 5000, the Vite development server serves the 
React app on port 5173 and proxies API calls to it, and MySQL listens on its default port 3306. 
No containerization or CI/CD pipeline was configured for this submission, since the course scope 
did not call for cloud deployment; Chapter 11 (Future Enhancements) outlines how this could be 
extended to a hosted environment. 

Page 10 
 
CHAPTER 5: DESIGN 
5.1 Database Design Principles 
The schema was normalized to remove redundant data: each fact is stored in exactly one place, 
and  every  relationship  between  entities  is  expressed  through  a  foreign  key  rather  than  by 
duplicating data across tables. Every table enforces its own invariants directly in the database — 
not just in application code — using PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, and CHECK 
constraints, so that invalid data (a negative capacity, an end time before a start time, a duplicate 
registration)  is  rejected  at  the  database  level  even  if  a  bug  elsewhere  in  the  application  tried  to 
insert it. 
5.2 ER Diagram / Database Schema 
The database consists of seven related tables, shown in Figure 5.1. 
 
USERS stores every account (student or admin) with a bcrypt-hashed password and a role flag. 
ROOMS holds the physical inventory  of bookable spaces — name, number, building, capacity, 
type, equipment, and status. EVENTS holds each event's details and an optional assigned room. 
REGISTRATIONS links a user to an event they have signed up for, with a UNIQUE constraint 
preventing the same student registering twice for the same event. ROOM_SCHEDULES holds the 
authoritative time-block for every room-event pairing and is the single table every conflict check 
reads from. BOOKINGS records who (which admin) made a given room assignment and when, 
serving   as   an   audit   trail   rather   than   a   second   source   of   truth   for   conflict-checking. 
OCCUPANCY_RECORDS stores expected, registered, and actual attendance figures per event, 
room, and date. 
5.3 Design Decisions and Assumptions 
Two design decisions were made explicitly, where the original entity list left some ambiguity, and 
are recorded here rather than left implicit in the code: 
 

Page 11 
 
• ROOM_SCHEDULES vs. BOOKINGS: since both tables could plausibly record “room + time,” 
ROOM_SCHEDULES  was  designated  the  single  source  of  truth  that  every  availability  check  and 
every  room-assignment  reads  from,  while  BOOKINGS  is  treated  purely  as  an  audit  trail  of  who 
performed the assignment. Both are written together, atomically, inside one database transaction, so 
they can never drift out of sync. 
• Effective registration capacity: the EVENTS table has no dedicated “maximum participants” field, so 
once a room is assigned to an event, that room's capacity is treated as the effective registration limit. 
Before a room is assigned, registration is left uncapped. 

Page 12 
 
CHAPTER 6: IMPLEMENTATION 
6.1 Module-wise Implementation 
The  backend  is  organized  into  six  resource  modules,  each  with  its  own  routes,  controller,  and 
model  file:  Authentication,  Rooms,  Events,  Registrations,  Bookings,  and  Occupancy.  The  most 
involved  piece  of  logic sits  in  the  Events  module's  room-assignment  function,  which  runs  four 
checks  in  sequence — the  room  exists  and  is  active,  its  capacity  is  sufficient  for  the  event's 
expected participants, and it has no conflicting schedule for the requested time — and only if all 
four pass does it atomically update the event's assigned room, write a new room_schedules row, 
and log a bookings row, inside a single database transaction so a failure partway through leaves 
no partial state behind. 
The core conflict-detection rule used throughout the system is: a requested time slot conflicts with 
an  existing  schedule  if  (existing_start  <  requested_end)  AND  (existing_end  >  requested_start). 
This single rule is applied consistently by the room-availability search, the event room-assignment 
workflow,  and  the  booking-creation  endpoint,  so  a  room  can  never  end  up  double-booked  no 
matter which entry point was used to book it. 
6.2 Front-end Logic 
The frontend uses React's Context API for the two pieces of state that genuinely need to be shared 
across  the  whole  application — the  logged-in  user  (AuthContext)  and  toast  notifications 
(ToastContext) — and  otherwise  keeps  state  local  to  the  component  that  needs  it.  This  was  a 
deliberate  choice  to  avoid  the  added  complexity  of  a  state-management  library  such  as  Redux, 
which was not necessary at this project's scale. Shared UI elements (a Modal, a ConfirmDialog, 
status badges, and loading/empty/error placeholders) are each written once and reused across every 
admin and student page, so every page in the app fails, loads, and confirms actions in a visually 
consistent way. 
6.3 API Integration 
All HTTP calls go through one central Axios instance, which automatically attaches the logged-in 
user's JWT to every outgoing request and automatically logs the user out if any response comes 
back with a 401 Unauthorized status (for example, after the token expires). Each backend resource 
has a matching frontend “service” file (roomService.js, eventService.js, and so on) so that no page 
ever hardcodes a URL or repeats the same fetch logic. 
6.4 Authentication and Authorization 
Registration always creates a student account — there is deliberately no way to create an admin 
account through the public API, so an attacker (or a curious student) cannot register their way into 
administrator  access.  Admin  accounts  exist  only  because  they  were  inserted  directly  into  the 
database. Every protected route runs a `protect` middleware that verifies the JWT, and admin-only 
routes additionally  run an `adminOnly` middleware that  checks the token's role claim, rejecting 
any student token with a 403 Forbidden response. 

Page 13 
 
CHAPTER 7: FEATURES 
7.1 List of Main Features 
Student-facing features: 
• Browse, search, and filter upcoming events by name and type 
• View full event details, including assigned room and capacity 
• Register for an event, with duplicate-registration and capacity limits enforced automatically 
• View “My Registrations” with live status (Registered / Cancelled / Attended) 
• Check room availability for any date and time window 
• View a personal profile 
Administrator-facing features: 
• Add,  edit,  and  safely  delete  rooms  (with  a  warning  before  shrinking  a  room's  capacity  below  what 
upcoming events need) 
• Add, edit, and delete events, and assign a room to an event 
• A live dashboard showing total rooms, rooms occupied right now, upcoming events, today's events, 
total registrations, and capacity warnings 
• View and manage all bookings, including cancellation 
• View all student registrations, filterable by event or status 
• Record and update occupancy after an event, with an automatically calculated occupancy percentage 
and status badge 
7.2 How Each Feature Works 
Room  availability  checking:  given  a  date,  a  start  time,  an  end  time,  and  an  optional  minimum 
capacity,  the  system  checks  every  room's  status  (excluding  Maintenance/Inactive  rooms),  its 
capacity,  and  whether  any  existing  room_schedules  entry  overlaps  the  requested  window, 
returning two lists — rooms that are available, and rooms that are not, each with a plain-English 
reason such as “Already booked for ‘AI Workshop’ from 10:00 AM to 12:00 PM.” 
 
Occupancy percentage calculation: once an admin records the actual headcount for an event, the 
system  computes  (actual_occupancy  ÷  room_capacity)  ×  100  and  buckets  the  result  into  one  of 

Page 14 
 
four labels: below 60% is “Normal,” 60–89% is “High,” 90–99% is “Near Capacity,” and 100% 
or above is “Over Capacity” — shown to the admin as a colored progress bar. 
Capacity-reduction warning: if an admin tries to reduce a room's capacity below what an upcoming 
event assigned to that room expects, the system does not silently allow it — it responds with the 
specific  list  of  affected  events  and  asks  the  admin  to  explicitly  confirm  before  the  change  is 
applied. 

Page 15 
 
CHAPTER 8: TESTING 
8.1 Postman API Testing 
A  complete  Postman  collection  was  built  covering  all  22  REST  endpoints,  organized  into  six 
folders  (Auth,  Rooms,  Events,  Registrations,  Bookings,  Occupancy)  plus  a  Health  check.  The 
Login requests carry a small test script that automatically saves the returned JWT into a collection 
variable, and requests such as Create Event, Assign Room, Register, and Create Occupancy Record 
are chained together using those variables, so a full workflow can be exercised without manually 
copying any ID or token between requests. 
8.2 Integration Testing 
Beyond  Postman,  the  system  was  tested  end-to-end  against  a  real,  running  MySQL  database  at 
every stage of development — each backend module was verified with the actual database before 
the next module was built on top of it, rather than being tested in isolation with mocked data. As 
a final integration check, the entire database was dropped and rebuilt from schema.sql and seed.sql 
from zero, and the full checklist below was re-run against that fresh install to confirm the system 
works correctly for a first-time setup, not just in an already-running development environment. 
8.3 Tools Used for Testing 
• Postman — manual and scripted API testing 
• curl (command line) — scripted regression testing across every phase of development 
• MySQL command-line client — direct verification of table contents and constraint behavior 
• Manual browser testing — verifying the React frontend's behavior and appearance

One test also uncovered a real defect rather than confirming correct behavior: pre-filling the Edit 
Event  form's  date/time  fields initially  used  the  API's  raw  UTC-encoded  timestamp  instead  of 
converting it to the browser's local time, which would have shown an incorrect time (for example, 
4:30 AM instead of 10:00 AM) on any machine not running in the UTC timezone. This is discussed 
further in Chapter 10. 

Page 17 
 
CHAPTER 9: DEPLOYMENT 
9.1 Steps to Deploy 
The application is deployed locally for development and demonstration as follows: 
• Load the schema and seed data: mysql -u root -p < database/schema.sql, then ... < database/seed.sql 
• Start the backend: cd server, npm install, npm run dev (listens on port 5000) 
• Start the frontend: cd client, npm install, npm run dev (listens on port 5173) 
• Open http://localhost:5173 in a browser and log in with a seeded account 
9.2 Environment Configuration

CHAPTER 10: CHALLENGES & LIMITATIONS 
10.1 Issues Faced During Development 
• Ambiguity between ROOM_SCHEDULES and BOOKINGS: the original data model included two 
tables that could both plausibly track “room + time,” which risked the two falling out of sync if both 
were updated independently. 
• A  timezone-conversion  bug:  the  Edit  Event  form's  date/time  fields  were  pre-filled  by  slicing  digits 
directly  out  of  the  API's  UTC-encoded  timestamp  string,  rather  than  converting  it  to  the  browser's 
local time first — correct only by coincidence when the server happens to run in the UTC timezone. 
• A MySQL startup failure (“unable to setup unix socket lock file”) encountered mid-development, 
caused by a stale mysqld process still holding the socket file after an earlier restart. 
10.2 Solutions Applied 
For  the ROOM_SCHEDULES/BOOKINGS  ambiguity,  a  clear  rule  was  adopted  and  enforced 
consistently in code: ROOM_SCHEDULES is the single source every conflict check reads from, 
and BOOKINGS is written at the same time, inside the same database transaction, purely as an 
audit trail — so the two can never disagree. 
For  the  timezone  bug,  a  small  shared  utility  (dateUtils.js)  was  written  that  converts  an  ISO 
timestamp to a form field's expected value using  JavaScript's local-time Date getters (getHours, 
getDate,  and  so  on) rather  than  UTC  getters  or  raw  string  slicing.  The  fix  was  verified  by 
deliberately simulating a non-UTC server timezone (Asia/Kolkata) and confirming the displayed 
time matched what was actually stored. 
For the MySQL startup failure, the stale process was terminated, the leftover socket and PID files 
were   removed,   and   the   service   was   restarted   cleanly — now   documented   as   a   known 
troubleshooting step in the project's README. 
10.3 Current Limitations or Known Bugs 
• No email verification or password-reset flow currently exists for user accounts. 
• Admin accounts can only be created by inserting a row directly into the database — by design, there 
is no public sign-up path to an admin role. 
• Actual occupancy must be entered manually by an admin after an event; there is no automatic check-
in mechanism (e.g. QR-code scanning). 
• The system has been tested on a single local deployment and has not yet been deployed to a public 
cloud environment.

 Abstract 
 
The Interview Practice Platform with AI Feedback (Intteree) is a full-stack web application designed to help 
students and job seekers practise technical, behavioral, HR, and system design interviews in a structured 
environment. Traditional interview preparation provides either static question banks or feedback that is delayed, 
subjective, or unavailable. The platform combines an interactive interview workflow with automated response 
evaluation and persistent performance tracking. Users create an account, select an interview category and target 
role, choose the number of questions, and complete a timed question-by-question practice session. Questions 
are sampled from a MongoDB-backed question bank. After a response is submitted, the backend sends the 
question, its ideal key points, and the candidate answer to an AI evaluation service powered by Google Gemini 
through the @google/genai SDK. The evaluator returns structured JSON feedback containing scores for 
relevance, clarity, confidence, communication, and overall performance, together with strengths, weaknesses, 
actionable suggestions, and a stronger example response. An optional webcam-based integrity proctoring 
module records focus loss during a session, and a browser Web Speech API option allows voice dictation of 
answers. The system stores interview sessions and feedback in MongoDB using Mongoose, protects application 
routes with JWT authentication, and provides dashboard and progress views for reviewing previous 
performance. A local heuristic fallback evaluator keeps feedback generation working when the Gemini service 
is unavailable or unconfigured. The result is a repeatable, database-backed interview practice environment that 
converts candidate answers into structured, actionable feedback.

CHAPTER -1 INTRODUCTION 
1.1 Background of the Project 
Interview preparation is often built around static question lists, repeated self-practice, or informal 
feedback from peers and mentors. These methods let a candidate rehearse answers, but they do not 
provide consistent evaluation after every attempt. A candidate may know that an answer "sounds 
weak" without knowing whether the problem is relevance, clarity, confidence, communication, or 
missing technical detail. 
The  Interview  Practice  Platform  with  AI  Feedback  developed  under  the  project  name  Intteree 
addresses this gap by turning interview practice  into a repeatable software workflow. Instead of 
acting as a general-purpose chatbot, the platform presents interview questions, records candidate 
answers,  evaluates  each  answer  against  structured  criteria,  and  stores  the  resulting  feedback  for 
later analysis. 
1.2 Problem Statement 
Traditional  interview  preparation  relies  on  practising  with  friends,  mentors,  or  reading  generic 
question banks. Feedback in these settings is frequently inconsistent, delayed, subjective, or simply 
unavailable,  and  candidates  lack  a  structured  way  to  measure  performance  on  standard  metrics 
such  as  clarity,  technical  accuracy,  and  communication  confidence.  The  system  must  therefore 
coordinate user authentication, question selection, timed response capture, AI evaluation, feedback 
persistence, session completion, and historical performance analytics reliably, and without failing 
when the external AI service is unreachable. 
1.3 Scope of the Project 
Account  registration,  login,  and  profile  information  including  target  role  and  experience  level. 
Interview configuration across Technical, Behavioral, HR, System Design and Mixed categories. 
Role-aware  question  sampling  with  a  configurable  question  count  between  1  and  10.  Timed 
question-by-question  response  capture  with  optional  browser  speech-to-text  dictation.  Optional 
webcam-based integrity proctoring that tracks focus loss during a session. AI evaluation through 
Gemini with a structured JSON response schema. Persistent storage of sessions, answers, scores, 
strengths,  weaknesses  and  suggestions.  Dashboard  and  progress  analytics  for  historical  score 
trends and recurring weaknesses. Real-time voice-to-voice avatar interviews, payment processing, 
and a verified public cloud deployment are treated as out of scope for this iteration; the platform 
focuses on accurate, asynchronous text and speech-to-text evaluation with analytics. 
1.4 Objectives 
• Provide a repeatable interview practice environment for students and job seekers. 
• Evaluate responses using consistent dimensions: relevance, clarity, confidence, communication and 
overall quality. 
• Generate understandable, structured feedback rather than an unstructured AI paragraph. 
• Reduce dependence on human evaluators for baseline mock interviews. 
• Persist interview history so users can review progress across multiple sessions. 

Page 10 
 
• Identify recurring weaknesses to guide future practice, maintaining a resilient fallback evaluator 
when Gemini is unavailable. 
 
 
1.5 Importance of the Application 
The application combines practice and evaluation in one workflow. It reduces the friction between 
answering  a  question  and  understanding  what  could  be  improved.  Because  feedback  is  stored 
against individual questions and sessions, the system can aggregate results instead of treating each 
practice attempt as an isolated interaction, letting a candidate see whether a weakness is improving 
over time. 
1.6 Target Users / Audience 
The system serves students and fresh graduates practising technical, behavioral, HR, and system 
design interviews; entry-level candidates targeting specific roles with timed sessions; job seekers 
using   repeated   practice   to   improve   interview   readiness;   and project   evaluators/faculty 
demonstrating full-stack architecture, database usage, API integration, and AI-assisted evaluation.

CHAPTER 3: TECHNOLOGY STACK 
3.1 Frontend

The  backend  is  a  REST  API  built  with  Node.js  and  Express.js,  structured  cleanly  into  routes,

3.4 Security & Version Control

3.5 Authentication and Security Libraries 
Passwords are hashed with bcrypt (10 salt rounds) before being stored — plain-text passwords are

CHAPTER 4: SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE 
4.1 High-Level Architecture Diagram 
The system follows a decoupled client-server architecture, with the AI evaluation service separated 
from  the  core  interview  workflow  logic.  Requests  flow  down  from  the  React  single-page 
application through the Express REST API layer to MongoDB and Google Gemini, and structured 
evaluation results flow back to the client. 
4.2 Description of Each Layer 
Presentation Layer: React provides login/register, dashboard, category and session configuration, 
the  interview  session,  the  feedback  result,  and  progress  views.  A  ProtectedRoute  component 
prevents access to application pages without an authenticated user. 
Application  Layer:  Express  exposes  authentication,  question,  interview,  feedback,  and  progress 
routes. Controllers validate requests, query MongoDB, call the AI service, and update session state. 
AI Evaluation Layer: aiService.js creates the  Gemini client and requests JSON output matching 
the  feedback  schema.  If  the  Gemini  key  is  unavailable  or  an  API  call  fails,  a  local  heuristic 
evaluator returns fallback feedback so a live session never crashes. 
4.3 AI Feedback Pipeline 
The candidate receives a sampled question and starts the response timer, submitting their answer 
by typing or speech-to-text dictation. The backend retrieves the ideal key points for the question 
and sends the payload to Google Gemini via @google/genai (using gemini-2.5-flash). The model 
returns   structured   JSON   containing   five   integer   scores   (relevance,   clarity,   confidence, 
communication, overall), strengths, weaknesses, actionable suggestions, and an improved example 
answer. The feedback is persisted in MongoDB and aggregated into overall session analytics. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
CHAPTER 5: DATABASE DESIGN 

Page 10 
 
5.1 Database Design Principles 
The  MongoDB  design  separates  account  information,  question-bank  content,  live  interview 
sessions,  and  generated  feedback.  The  schema  uses  document  referencing  (ObjectIds)  via 
Mongoose  rather  than  deep  embedding,  which  keeps  the  session  document  compact  and avoids 
document-size limits when extensive historical feedback is stored. References between documents 
allow  question  and  feedback  information  to  be  populated  when  a  session  is  retrieved,  and 
uniqueness is enforced on user emails while passwords are hashed through a pre-save hook. 
5.2 Data Model and Core Entities 
The  database  consists  of four  primary  Mongoose  collections:  User,  Question,  InterviewSession,  and 
Feedback. 
User: Stores name, unique email, bcrypt password hash, target role, and experience level. Question: 
Stores text, category (Technical, Behavioral, HR, System Design, Mixed), target role, difficulty, 
ideal  key  points  array,  and  tags.  InterviewSession:  References  User  and  Question  ObjectIds, 
tracking  session  category,  status,  submitted  answers,  response  durations,  proctoring  integrity 
events, and overall score out of 100. Feedback: References session, question, and user ObjectIds, 
storing five individual evaluation scores (relevance, clarity, confidence, communication, overall), 
lists  for  strengths,  weaknesses,  and  actionable  suggestions,  an  improved  example  response,  and 
raw model output. 
5.3 Design Decisions and Assumptions 
Key architectural and database design decisions include: 
• Question Selection: MongoDB aggregation ($sample) randomly selects questions filtered by category 
and target role during session initialization. 
• Feedback  Isolation:  AI  feedback  is  stored  in  a  separate  Feedback  collection  and  referenced  in  the 
session, keeping session documents lightweight while preserving full evaluation history. 
CHAPTER 6: IMPLEMENTATION 
6.1 Module-wise Implementation 
The  backend  is  organized  into  core  resource  modules:  Authentication  (JWT  &  bcrypt  password 
hashing), Question Management (sampling & filters), Interview Session Management (lifecycle & 
answer submission), AI Evaluation (Gemini 2.5 Flash SDK integration & local heuristic fallback), 
Feedback   Management,   and   Progress   Analytics   (trend   calculation   &   recurring   weakness 
extraction). 
When an answer is submitted via POST /api/interviews/:sessionId/answer, the interview controller 
passes the question details, ideal key points, and candidate response to aiService.js. The AI service 
uses the @google/genai SDK with responseSchema enforcement to return typed JSON, which is 
immediately saved as a Feedback document and linked to the session. 
 
6.2 Front-end Logic

The  React  single-page  application  uses  AuthContext  for  user  state,  Axios  with  Bearer  token 
interceptors,  and  React  Router  DOM.  ProtectedRoute  components  block  unauthenticated  users. 
The InterviewSession component manages the question progression, response timer, browser Web

HTTP requests are handled by a central Axios client. API calls are grouped into dedicated service

Authentication  utilizes  stateless  JSON  Web  Tokens  (JWT).  Passwords  are  pre-hashed  using 
bcryptjs  with  10  salt  rounds.  Backend  middleware  verifies  the  Bearer  token  on  every  protected

CHAPTER 9: DEPLOYMENT 
9.1 Steps to Deploy 
To launch the Intteree application locally for development and demonstration: 
• Seed the database: Run `npm run seed` in backend directory to populate questions into MongoDB 
• Start the backend API server: `cd server && npm install && npm run dev` (Port 5000) 
• Start the React client: `cd client && npm install && npm run dev` (Port 5173) 
• Open http://localhost:5173 in Chrome or Edge to access the application 
9.2 Environment Configuration 
Environment  variables  are  configured  via  server/.env  (using  .env.example  as  a  committed 
template): PORT=5000, MONGO_URI=mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/interview_platform, 
JWT_SECRET=<secret_key>,    JWT_EXPIRES_IN=7d,    GEMINI_API_KEY=<gemini_key>, 
GEMINI_MODEL=gemini-2.5-flash, and CLIENT_URL=http://localhost:5173. 
9.3 Hosting of Frontend and Backend 
For demonstration, both Express and Vite run as separate local processes, with Vite proxying /api 
requests   to   port   5000.   In   production,   MongoDB   Atlas   handles   database   persistence, 
Render/Heroku hosts the backend API, and Vercel/Netlify hosts the static React build. 
CHAPTER 10: CHALLENGES & LIMITATIONS 
10.1 Issues Faced During Development 
• Enforcing Structured Output: Unstructured LLM text outputs initially caused JSON parsing errors in 
backend controllers. 
• External  Dependency  Risks:  Network  latency  or rate  limiting  from  external  Gemini  API  endpoints 
could freeze interactive practice sessions. 
• Browser Speech API Variations: Web Speech API dictation demonstrated inconsistent behavior across 
non-Chromium web browsers. 
10.2 Solutions Applied 
Migrated to the latest @google/genai SDK, passing a strict responseSchema configuration to force 
deterministic JSON output format matching the feedback model. 
Engineered a  local  heuristic  fallback  evaluator  that  computes  bounded  scores  based  on  answer 
length and key point keyword matching whenever the Gemini API is unreachable. 
 
 
 
10.3  Current Limitations 
• Text and dictation evaluation cannot capture non-verbal cues, tone of voice, or body language.

• Gemini evaluation relies on active internet access; fallback evaluator provides simpler heuristics. 
• Public cloud deployment, email verification, and password-reset flows are omitted in this iteration.
